column2: All-cause SSI cost (upper bound): m_ssi_cost = 1.000, i.e. Edmiston's regression-adjusted ALL-CAUSE incremental payment charged at face value
column30: **A2 INVERTED THIS ROW (2026-08-17).** It used to be the attribution-adjusted SENSITIVITY, run at m_ssi_cost = k_attrib_pennington while the base case charged Edmiston's all-cause increment. Verification of Edmiston's full text established that its payments are least-squares means from a GLM with log link and gamma error, covariate-adjusted only, over ALL-CAUSE total payments, with NO MATCHING anywhere in the paper -- an upper bound on SSI-attributable cost by construction, because the residual gap is confounding by indication. The matched anchor therefore became the BASE CASE, and this row now carries the all-cause UPPER BOUND. Keeping it at the old value would have made it a numerical duplicate of the base case. It scales all six marginal tranches together and remains the single largest swing in the model; because the averted cost is larger here, ciNPWT appears to pay off at a LOWER baseline risk -- which is exactly why it is a bound and not the headline.

column2: ciNPWT prevents SUPERFICIAL SSI only: no benefit on deep SSI (Zwanenburg 2020 [11] RCT subgroup)
column30:
**ADDED BY THE A2 AUDIT, AND IT IS THE MOST ADVERSE SCENARIO IN THIS FILE.** Zwanenburg 2020 [11] -- the source of the base-case RR 0.61 -- reports NO significant benefit for deep SSI in its randomized trials, and its authors write that 'iNPWT efficacy may potentially be limited to superficial SSIs only, and such SSIs are of less clinical relevance than deep SSIs.' This model draws the large majority of its saving from averted DEEP SSI, so that subgroup result is a first-order threat to its logic and is tested here rather than left in prose.
HOW IT IS IMPLEMENTED, AND WHY THIS IS EXACT RATHER THAN AN APPROXIMATION. The engine applies RR to the TOTAL SSI risk and splits the result by frac_deep / frac_sup, so it cannot be told to spare deep SSI directly. But INMB is a DIFFERENCE between arms. If ciNPWT does not prevent deep SSI then deep cases are equinumerous in both arms and every deep cost and every deep QALY loss CANCELS from the incremental. Setting the three deep cost tranches and du_deep to zero in BOTH arms makes them cancel too, and leaves the superficial contribution untouched: superficial cases averted are p x frac_sup x (1 - RR) either way. The two formulations therefore give a NEARLY identical INMB. Measured against the exact counterfactual (arm B run at RR_eff = RR x f_sup + f_deep with the split re-weighted so the deep hazard is unchanged and the superficial hazard is scaled by RR), this emulation agrees to within 1.3% and ERRS AGAINST ciNPWT's critics -- i.e. the exact counterfactual is slightly MORE adverse at every stratum (-$209.26/-$115.57/-$17.79 exact vs -$209.22/-$115.43/-$17.57 here). The residual gap is competing risk: the two depths draw from the same Well pool over the three-cycle onset window, so sparing deep SSI in arm B leaves marginally less mass available to generate superficial onsets than this emulation retains. Exactness would additionally require du_recovered_residual = 0 (it is 0.00 in the base case but 0.06 in the residual-decrement scenario, and the two tunnels differ in length, so arrival into RECOVERED is depth-dependent) and depth-independent mortality (which does hold here). The sign is negative at every stratum under BOTH formulations, so the reversal finding is safe. This row also distorts each arm's absolute cost and QALY LEVELS, and its nnt / ssi_prevented_per_1000 / reop_prevented_per_1000 columns are the BASE-CASE counts because the trace is untouched -- only the incremental columns of this row may be quoted.

column2: Medicare perspective: the six *_mcr cost tranches replace the commercial set (2 y horizon)
column30: **A2 CORRECTED THIS ROW (2026-08-17) AND RETIRED ITS FOOTNOTE.** This build stated that Edmiston reports the Medicare SUPERFICIAL payment at 6 months only, and extrapolated the 12- and 24-month tranches by transferring the commercial growth ratio onto the 6-month value ($3,259 and $3,124). All three Medicare superficial payments are reported -- $11,044, $17,967 and $24,096 -- in four places, so the correct marginal tranches are $6,923 and $6,129, each roughly TWICE what was used. The extrapolation also failed in principle: Medicare payments grow FASTER than commercial from 6 to 12 months (1.627 vs 1.295), so a transferred commercial ratio understates them. **Every dollar in this row is now a reported Edmiston value**, the four-tranche identity 11,044 + 6,923 + 6,129 = 24,096 closes exactly, and no extrapolation footnote is required.

column2: Spine-specific effect (favorable): RR = 0.434 (Chen 2022 [8])
column30: Chen pools 5 small retrospective spine studies (n=994) and reports an ODDS ratio, applied here as a risk ratio; at p of 0.5-15% the two differ by at most a few percent and the direction (an OR sits further from 1 than the RR) makes this favorable scenario slightly MORE favorable to ciNPWT. column2: Residual decrement: du_recovered_residual = 0.06 in RECOV to the horizon (2 y)
column30: A GENUINE EVIDENCE CONFLICT, which is why it is a scenario and not a DSA row. Urquhart 2021 [21] reports PROM recovery by 1 year (the base case: RECOV = WELL); McFarland 2023 [19] reports a persisting decrement, and Freire-Archer [17] reports up-to-25% persistent infection. This conflict is the only reason RECOV is kept as a state distinct from WELL. Arm A sends more patients through the tunnels into RECOV, so a residual decrement penalises the comparator and favours ciNPWT -- and the effect GROWS with the horizon.

column2: Decolonization secondary analysis: residual-risk multiplier (1 - f_SA) + f_SA x OR_decol = 0.54 + 0.46 x 0.56 = 0.798; the stratum p is treated as the PRE-decolonization risk
column30: Universal S. aureus decolonization is background in BOTH arms (SHEA/IDSA essential practice for implant procedures), so its cost and its effect CANCEL from every base-case increment. It survives only here, as one transparent line: it lowers the risk each patient brings to the ciNPWT decision, and the reported question is how far that shifts patients BELOW the ciNPWT threshold. p shown is the RESIDUAL risk actually run (= stratum p x 0.798); p_stratum is the pre-decolonization risk. LIMITATION: ciNPWT's relative risk is assumed to apply equally to the residual SSI pool, which is relatively more gram-negative and polymicrobial after S. aureus is selectively removed. `decol_residual_attenuated` relaxes exactly that assumption.

column2: Societal perspective (productivity loss, patient/caregiver time, travel)
column30: NOT RUN -- no societal cost input exists anywhere in the parameter store. The declared perspective is the US commercial payer on a payments basis (Medicare is the alternative payer scenario above); adding productivity or caregiver costs would require inventing them. Direction if it were run is unambiguous: SSI carries substantial productivity loss that the payer perspective ignores, so a societal perspective would raise the cost per SSI averted and move the threshold DOWN, making ciNPWT look better. The payer perspective is therefore the conservative one. Documented as unrun and data-limited.

column2: 'Risk-targeted ciNPWT' as a separately modelled third arm
column30: NOT RUN BY DESIGN -- and this is a plan decision, not a limitation of this script. A third arm that treats only patients above a risk threshold requires the POPULATION DISTRIBUTION of predicted 90-day SSI risk, which does not exist in the evidence base. Rather than invent one, risk-targeted ciNPWT is reported as a DERIVED result: the per-stratum rows in this file plus `budget_impact.csv`, which is parameterized by the proportion of the programme treated. That is MATHEMATICALLY IDENTICAL to a third arm whose targeting rule selects the same proportion at the same risk, and it avoids fabricating a distribution.
